scenario_stem:
Amber Grove Juices is a private limited company in Country X that presses cold-pressed mango and passionfruit juice. Sales of its signature mango juice have risen from 40,000 bottles in 2023 to 68,000 bottles in 2025, a growth-stage product life cycle. The owner, Lena Duarte, employs 14 staff and sells mainly through 30 independent grocers and one supermarket chain across two regions.

The supermarket has offered to stock mango juice in 45 more stores if Amber Grove installs a second bottling line costing $90,000. Alternatively, Lena could spend $18,000 on a regional television and social media advertising campaign to lift sales further. Either option risks stretching cash flow this year, and the mango juice is entering late growth, so she must decide quickly before summer demand peaks.

questions.question_text: Define 'growth stage' of the product life cycle.
questions.model_answer: The growth stage is the stage of the product life cycle when sales rise rapidly and the product becomes more widely known, so revenue and usually profit increase [2].

knowledge_max_2: sales rise rapidly after introduction as the product gains acceptance
revenue and profit increase as sales grow

questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Rising sales grow revenue [k], because bottle sales rose from 40,000 in 2023 to 68,000 in 2025 [app]. Benefit 2: A strong growth-stage product attracts bigger distribution deals [k], shown by the supermarket offer to stock mango juice in 45 more stores [app].

knowledge_max_2: growth stage brings rising revenue/profit

application_max_2: bottle sales rose from 40,000 in 2023 to 68,000 in 2025

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Amber Grove Juices might face as its mango juice enters late growth.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Production capacity may not keep pace with demand [k], because sales rose from 40,000 to 68,000 bottles a year on one line [app], risking empty shelves that could cost the new supermarket contract and the 30 grocers [an]. Problem 2: Cash flow could be stretched by expansion [k], because the $90,000 bottling line and $18,000 campaign both absorb cash this year [app], leaving Amber Grove short of working capital before summer demand peaks [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Amber Grove Juices should install the second bottling line rather than spend $18,000 on advertising? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One side is that the second bottling line locks in growth [k], because the supermarket will stock mango juice in 45 more stores once it is installed [app], turning current capacity into supply for over two regions and converting 68,000-bottle sales into lasting profit [an]. On the other hand, advertising is far cheaper [k]: $18,000 spreads the word across the region without borrowing and keeps options open if growth slows [app], making it a lower-risk way to push mango juice before it exits late growth [an]. Overall, the bottling line is the better choice because $90,000 unlocks 45 more stores of guaranteed distribution, a much larger prize than the $18,000 campaign can deliver [eval], although Amber Grove should only proceed if cash flow stays positive and sales hold above 60,000 bottles a year [eval].

scenario_stem:
Old Harbour Biscuits is a partnership in Country X making digestive and ginger biscuits since 2004. Its best-selling digestive biscuit sells 120,000 packs a year at $2.40 each; after years of maturity, sales have been flat for 3 years and the market is saturated. The two partners employ 22 staff and supply 55 independent grocers and 8 cafes across the southern region, with profits easing from $96,000 to $70,000 a year.

The partners are considering two options: relaunching the digestive biscuit with three new flavours and a modern wrapper costing $45,000, or cutting the price by 15% to $2.04 to stimulate sales. Their main competitor cut prices last year and gained 8% market share. They cannot afford both options and must decide by the end of the month.

questions.model_answer: Saturation is the stage of the product life cycle when the market is full of the product, sales stop rising and competition is intense, so revenue flattens [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems a saturated market creates for Old Harbour Biscuits.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Flat sales cap revenue [k], because digestive biscuit sales have been stuck at 120,000 packs a year for 3 years [app]. Problem 2: Rivals undercut and take share [k], because the main competitor cut prices and gained 8% market share [app].

questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A relaunch can re-stimulate demand [k], because three new flavours and a modern wrapper give existing buyers a reason to try the biscuits again [app], which can reverse 3 years of flat sales supplied to 55 grocers and 8 cafes [an]. Benefit 2: Fresh packaging can support a better price [k], because buyers link modern packaging with improved quality [app], lifting margins as profits eased from $96,000 to $70,000 and offsetting the $45,000 wrapper cost [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Old Harbour Biscuits should relaunch with new flavours rather than cut the price by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One side is that relaunching refreshes the product [k], because three new flavours and a modern wrapper costing $45,000 give buyers a reason to repurchase [app], reviving the 120,000-pack-a-year business and rebuilding profits that eased from $96,000 to $70,000 [an]. On the other hand, the 15% price cut to $2.04 is simpler and faster [k]: it directly answers the competitor that gained 8% market share and could lift volume quickly [app], but each pack earns $0.36 less, so profit per pack falls [an]. Overall, the relaunch is the better choice because cutting price only matches a rival and erodes margins, while new flavours defend share properly and could restore the $96,000 peak profit level [eval], but the partners should track sales weekly and switch to pricing action if the relaunch has not lifted packs within 3 months [eval].

scenario_stem:
Everline Audio is a private limited company in Country X that has manufactured DVD players and MP3 players for 11 years. Sales peaked at 30,000 units in 2021 and fell to 9,000 units in 2025, placing both products in the decline stage of the product life cycle. The business employs 38 staff, holds $260,000 of unsold stock, and annual revenue has halved from $2.4 million to $1.2 million over three years.

The directors are considering either an extension strategy, releasing a combined DVD/MP3 media centre with smart streaming for $120,000 of retooling, or discontinuing the range and selling the factory machinery to raise about $180,000. Either decision will affect the 38 employees, and the shareholders will vote on the plan next month.

questions.model_answer: The decline stage is when sales fall steadily because the product is outdated or replaced by alternatives, and revenue and profit shrink [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Everline Audio's products are in the decline stage.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Technology is outdated [k], because DVD players and MP3 players have been replaced by streaming and online content [app]. Reason 2: Unit sales keep shrinking [k], with sales falling from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units in 2025 [app].

knowledge_max_2: products become outdated as technology moves on

application_max_2: DVD/MP3 players replaced by modern alternatives

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Everline Audio of launching the media centre as an extension strategy.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: It can win back lapsed customers [k], because a DVD/MP3 media centre with smart streaming updates the old range for existing owners [app], slowing the slide from 30,000 units to 9,000 units a year and protecting the 38 staff [an]. Benefit 2: It keeps the factory productive [k], because $120,000 of retooling reuses the plant and 11 years of manufacturing experience [app], preserving $1.2 million of annual revenue instead of shutting down for a machinery sale [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Everline Audio should launch the media centre rather than discontinue the range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One side is that the extension strategy buys time [k], because the media centre with smart streaming refreshes an outdated range for only $120,000 of retooling [app], which could recover some of the fall from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units and keep the 38 staff employed [an]. On the other hand, discontinuing is cleaner [k], because selling the machinery for about $180,000 frees cash and ends the $260,000 unsold-stock problem [app], letting shareholders redeploy money instead of backing a shrinking DVD/MP3 market [an]. Overall, Everline should discontinue the range because four years of decline, down to 9,000 units from a 30,000 peak, show demand is structurally gone; taking the $180,000 is safer than risking $120,000 of further losses [eval], but if confirmed pre-orders for the media centre top 12,000 units the board should approve the launch instead [eval].

scenario_stem:

It employs 26 staff and its existing range is popular but flat. A supermarket chain wants Butterwick to supply a new sugar-free yogurt, with new product development costing $140,000 over 12 months, including testing, market research and packaging design.

If successful, the supermarket estimates the sugar-free yogurt could sell 60,000 pots a month at $2.20 per pot within a year. The creamery has $90,000 in the bank and would need to borrow the rest as a bank loan at 9% interest over 5 years. Owner Elena Vasquez must decide whether the new product is worth the cost and risk.

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: High up-front costs [k], because development costs $140,000 over 12 months including testing, research and packaging design [app], which must be paid before any sugar-free sales arrive [an]. Problem 2: It needs debt [k], because the creamery has only $90,000 in the bank and must borrow the rest at 9% over 5 years [app], so repayments strain the cash flow from flat $1.80-pot revenue [an].

Overall, Butterwick should develop the yogurt because the supermarket estimate implies $132,000 of monthly revenue against a $50,000 loan, an exceptional payback if even 50% of forecast is achieved [eval], but only after securing written supermarket volumes and staged loan drawdowns to cap losses if demand disappoints [eval].

Its flagship Silver Dragon tea sells 22,000 boxes a year at $9.60 per box, well above supermarket teas at $3.20 a box. Repeat customers account for 70% of sales, built on its strong brand image and consistent quality. The business employs 17 staff and exports to 6 countries across Europe and Asia.

A large retailer has asked Silvermist to cut the Silver Dragon price to $7.00 per box to match rivals, or invest $35,000 in a brand campaign to defend premium pricing. Sales fell 6% last year after a rival copied the foil packaging. The directors must decide before the spring selling season begins.

Reason 2: A distinct image is hard for rivals to copy [k], because the Silver Dragon brand took since 2016 to build through packaging and export reputation [app].

Problem 2: It cuts margins sharply [k], because each box earns $2.60 less than at $9.60 [app], which on 22,000 boxes a year removes about $57,200 of annual revenue [an].

On the other hand, the brand campaign defends the premium position [k], because $35,000 invested in reinforcing the Silver Dragon image protects the $9.60 price and the 70% repeat-purchase base [app], which funds exports to 6 countries and premium margins [an]. scenario_stem:
Petal & Thyme Organic Teas is a partnership in Country X selling herbal infusions in 12 flavours since 2019. They are choosing between two redesigns: a premium matte-black pouch with a resealable zip costing $0.52 per pouch, or a cheaper recyclable paper pouch at $0.28 per pouch for eco-conscious buyers and younger customers. Packaging is printed in batches of 20,000, and the chosen design will be on shelves for 3 years.

scenario_stem:
Northpeak Outdoor is a private limited company in Country X making hiking jackets since 2013. Its Northpeak Pro jacket sells 8,500 units a year at $145, with 45% of buyers reordering from 40 specialist outdoor shops across the highlands. The brand is known for its durability and a premium image built over 13 years, and the business employs 31 staff across design, sewing and distribution centres.

A budget rival entered at $95 per jacket and Northpeak sales fell 18% last quarter. The directors debate cutting the Northpeak Pro to $110 to defend sales volume against the rival, or keeping $145 and spending $60,000 on athlete sponsorship and a 'buy once, last forever' campaign to reinforce the premium brand image among loyal customers.

scenario_stem:
Velvet Cocoa Chocolatiers is a partnership in Country X making hand-crafted chocolate truffles for gifting since 2015. It sells 14,000 boxes a year at $18 per box, worth $252,000 in annual sales, and employs 12 staff across the kitchen, packing and retail counter. The partners plan a winter gift range in recyclable, plastic-free boxes costing $1.40 per box, up from $0.85 for the current boxes.

A trial of 400 customers showed 62% prefer recyclable packaging and would pay $20 per box. Developing the range needs $75,000 for new moulds and packaging design. Alternatively, the partners could refresh the existing range for $25,000 with new flavours but keep plastic packaging for existing corporate buyers. Autumn orders to corporate buyers are due in 10 weeks.
